chunks.text: CLINICAL GUIDELINE: ACNE VULGARIS & ROSACEA MANAGEMENT

1. ACNE VULGARIS PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the pilosebaceous units. Key pathogenic factors include:
- Hyperkeratinization of the follicular infundibulum causing microcomedones.
- Sebaceous gland hypersecretion stimulated by androgens.
- Proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes).
- Follicular inflammation and rupture causing inflammatory papules, pustules, nodules, and cysts.

CLINICAL CLASSIFICATION:
- Comedonal Acne: Open comedones (blackheads) and closed comedones (whiteheads). First-line treatment: Topical retinoids (adapalene 0.1%, tretinoin 0.025%-0.05%).
- Mild-to-Moderate Inflammatory Acne: Papules and pustules. First-line therapy: Benzoyl peroxide (2.5%-5%) combined with topical clindamycin (1%) or topical retinoids.
- Severe Nodulocystic Acne: Painful deep cysts, scarring risk. Requires systemic therapy: Oral isotretinoin or oral antibiotics (doxycycline, minocycline) under dermatological supervision.

2. ROSACEA SUBTYPES & DISTINCTION
Rosacea is a facial dermatosis characterized by flushing, erythema, and telangiectasia. Unlike acne, comedones are ABSENT.
- Erythematotelangiectatic Rosacea: Persistent central facial erythema, flushing, visible telangiectasias. Avoid spicy food, alcohol, hot drinks, UV radiation. Treatment: Topical brimonidine, oxymetazoline, vascular laser (PDL).
- Papulopustular Rosacea: Central erythema with inflammatory papules and pustules resembling acne without comedones. Treatment: Topical ivermectin 1%, metronidazole 0.75%, azelaic acid 15%-20%, low-dose oral doxycycline (40mg modified release).
- Phymatous Rosacea: Tissue hypertrophy (rhinophyma on the nose). Requires surgical or ablative laser intervention.
- Ocular Rosacea: Blepharitis, conjunctivitis, dryness, foreign body sensation.

3. DIETARY AND LIFESTYLE TRIGGERS
- High-glycemic-load diets increase IGF-1 and stimulate sebum production.
- Skim milk and whey protein powders are associated with acne flare-ups.
- Recommend omega-3 fatty acids, green tea polyphenols, zinc, and gentle non-comedogenic foaming cleansers.
CLINICAL GUIDELINE: ATOPIC DERMATITIS, CONTACT DERMATITIS & ECZEMA

1. ATOPIC DERMATITIS (ECZEMA)
Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, pruritic inflammatory skin disease associated with epidermal barrier disruption (often filaggrin gene mutations) and immune dysregulation (Th2-skewed response).
- Cardinal Symptom: Intense pruritus ("the itch that rashes").
- Morphological Hallmark: Ill-defined erythema, microvesiculation, oozing, crusting in acute phases; lichenification (skin thickening with exaggerated markings) in chronic phases.
- Distribution: Flexural surfaces (antecubital and popliteal fossae), neck, wrists in adults; cheeks, extensor surfaces in infants.

2. SEBORRHEIC DERMATITIS
Inflammatory disorder associated with Malassezia yeast colonization in sebaceous-rich areas.
- Presentation: Greasy yellowish scales overlying erythematous patches on scalp (dandruff), nasolabial folds, glabella, eyebrows, and ears.
- Treatment: Topical antifungal shampoos (ketoconazole 2%, selenium sulfide, zinc pyrithione), mild topical corticosteroids (hydrocortisone 1%), or topical calcineurin inhibitors.

3. CONTACT DERMATITIS
- Irritant Contact Dermatitis (ICD): Non-immunologic direct chemical/physical damage (soaps, detergents, wet work). Hands most commonly affected.
- Allergic Contact Dermatitis (ACD): Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction (nickel in jewelry, fragrances, poison ivy/urushiol, preservatives). Requires patch testing.

4. THERAPEUTIC REGIMEN FOR BARRIER REPAIR
- Cornerstone: Frequent application of bland ceramide-rich emollients (ointments or creams over lotions). Apply within 3 minutes of warm bathing ("soak and seal").
- Anti-inflammatory: Low-to-mid potency topical corticosteroids (hydrocortisone, triamcinolone acetonide) for acute flares. Transition to topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) for sensitive facial areas to avoid steroid-induced skin atrophy.
- Systemic / Biologics: Dupilumab (anti-IL-4R-alpha), JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib) for moderate-to-severe refractory cases.
CLINICAL GUIDELINE: CUTANEOUS FUNGAL, BACTERIAL & VIRAL INFECTIONS

1. DERMATOPHYTE INFECTIONS (TINEA)
Infections caused by dermatophyte fungi (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) digesting stratum corneum keratin.
- Tinea Corporis (Ringworm): Annular (ring-shaped) erythematous plaque with active elevated, scaly advancing border and central clearing.
- Tinea Cruris ("Jock Itch"): Pruritic erythematous plaques in the groin and upper thighs, sparing the scrotum (crucial distinction from cutaneous candidiasis which involves the scrotum and has satellite pustules).
- Tinea Pedis (Athlete's Foot): Interdigital maceration, fissuring, scaling on soles ("moccasin distribution").
- Tinea Capitis: Scaling, patchy alopecia with broken "black dot" hairs on scalp. Requires systemic oral griseofulvin or terbinafine (topical therapy is ineffective for follicular hair shaft infection).
- Diagnostic Confirmation: KOH wet mount microscopy demonstrating branching hyphae.

2. PITYRIASIS VERSICOLOR (TINEA VERSICOLOR)
Superficial infection by Malassezia globosa/furfur.
- Presentation: Hypopigmented or hyperpigmented, finely scaling macules coalescing on chest, back, and shoulders. More visible after sun exposure.
- Management: Topical selenium sulfide shampoo, ketoconazole 2% cream, or oral fluconazole.

3. BACTERIAL INFECTIONS
- Impetigo: Highly contagious superficial Staphylococcus aureus / Streptococcus pyogenes infection. Honey-colored crusts around mouth and nose in children. Treatment: Topical mupirocin 2% or oral cephalexin.
- Folliculitis: Erythematous follicular pustules centered on hair shafts.
- Cellulitis: Spreading erythema, warmth, edema, and tenderness of deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Systemic fever often present; requires systemic antibiotics.

4. VIRAL DERMATOSES
- Herpes Simplex (HSV-1 / HSV-2): Grouped painful vesicles on an erythematous base ("dewdrops on a rose petal"), transitioning to crusts. Oral valacyclovir or acyclovir.
- Herpes Zoster (Shingles): Reactivation of Varicella Zoster Virus along a single unilateral dermatome. Severe prodromal neuropathic pain preceding vesicular eruption. Early antiviral initiation within 72 hours reduces post-herpetic neuralgia risk.
- Verruca Vulgaris (Warts): Human Papillomavirus (HPV) induced hyperkeratotic, exophytic papules with thrombosed capillary black dots. Cryotherapy or salicylic acid.
CLINICAL GUIDELINE: GENERAL CUTANEOUS HEALTH, NUTRITION & EMERGENCY RED FLAGS

1. EVIDENCE-BASED DERMATOLOGICAL NUTRITION
- Anti-inflammatory Omega-3 Fatty Acids: EPA and DHA suppress pro-inflammatory leukotriene B4 (LTB4) and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2). Abundant in salmon, sardines, walnuts, and chia seeds.
- Zinc: Essential cofactor for matrix metalloproteinases, protein synthesis, and wound epithelialization. Promotes neutrophil and macrophage function.
- Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid): Obligate cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase in collagen synthesis. Scavenges free radicals from UV radiation.
- Vitamin D: Modulates antimicrobial peptides (cathelicidin LL-37) and suppresses overactive helper T-cell proliferation in psoriatic skin.
- Hydration & Skin Barrier: Maintaining hydration supports the stratum corneum natural moisturizing factor (NMF) consisting of amino acids, pyrrolidone carboxylic acid, and lactate.

2. SUN PROTECTION FACTOR (SPF) CLINICAL GUIDELINES
- Broad-Spectrum SPF 30 to 50+: Protects against UVB (erythema, direct DNA thymine dimers) and UVA (photoaging, reactive oxygen species, deep collagen degradation).
- Reapplication rule: Apply 2 mg/cm^2 (roughly one teaspoon for face and neck) 15-30 minutes prior to UV exposure, and reapply every 2 hours or immediately following swimming or sweating.

3. DERMATOLOGICAL RED FLAGS (IMMEDIATE PHYSICIAN / EMERGENCY ESCALATION)
The presence of any of the following symptoms warrants immediate in-person dermatological evaluation or emergency care:
- Systemic involvement: Skin rash accompanied by high fever, hypotension, or altered mental status.
- Rapid epidermal detachment: Painful denudation, skin blistering or sloughing covering >10% of body surface area (Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis). Positive Nikolsky sign.
- Rapidly progressive necrotizing soft tissue infection: Extreme disproportionate pain, purpura, crepitus, or woody induration (necrotizing fasciitis).
- Targetoid / Iris lesions with mucosal ulceration (oral, genital, conjunctival involvement) suggestive of Erythema Multiforme Major.
- Petechiae or purpura that do NOT blanch under diascopy pressure (glass slide test), indicating potential meningococcal septicemia or vasculitis.
CLINICAL GUIDELINE: PIGMENTARY DISORDERS & CUTANEOUS NEOPLASMS

1. MELASMA & HYPERPIGMENTATION
- Melasma: Acquired hypermelanosis predominantly affecting sun-exposed facial zones (malar cheeks, forehead, upper lip) in women of Fitzpatrick III-V skin types. Hormonal triggers (pregnancy, oral contraceptives) and UVA/visible blue light.
- Management: Strict broad-spectrum mineral sunscreen (SPF 50+ with iron oxides for visible light protection), topical hydroquinone 2%-4%, azelaic acid 20%, tranexamic acid, cysteamine.
- Post-Inflammatory Hyperpigmentation (PIH): Flat macular hyperpigmentation developing at sites of healed inflammatory lesions (acne, eczema, trauma). Gentle exfoliation with azelaic acid or niacinamide; avoid picking or harsh chemical peels.

2. VITILIGO & HYPOPIGMENTATION
- Vitiligo: Autoimmune destruction of epidermal melanocytes causing sharply circumscribed, amelanotic milky-white macules and patches.
- Management: Topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.1%), topical JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib cream), and targeted narrowband UVB phototherapy.

3. CUTANEOUS NEOPLASMS & THE ABCDE OF MELANOMA
The ABCDE clinical screening criteria for suspicious pigmented lesions:
- A: Asymmetry (one half does not match the other).
- B: Border Irregularity (scalloped, notched, or poorly defined edges).
- C: Color Variegation (heterogeneous shades of brown, black, red, white, or blue).
- D: Diameter (>6 mm, roughly pencil eraser size, though early melanomas can be smaller).
- E: Evolving (any change in size, shape, color, bleeding, itching, or rapid crusting).

4. NON-MELANOMA SKIN CANCERS
- Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC): Most common skin cancer. Pearly, translucent papule with telangiectasia, rolled borders, and central depression/ulceration. Highly curable with surgical excision (Mohs surgery).
- Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC): Hyperkeratotic, indurated erythematous papule or plaque, often with central ulceration or crusting. Arises frequently from precursor Actinic Keratoses on chronic sun-damaged skin.
- Seborrheic Keratosis (BENIGN): "Stuck-on", waxy, verrucous brown or tan plaques with pseudohorn cysts. Completely benign; no malignancy risk.
CLINICAL GUIDELINE: PSORIASIS VULGARIS & SCALING ERYTHEMAS

1. PSORIASIS VULGARIS PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated, systemic inflammatory disease driven by the IL-23/IL-17 immune axis, resulting in keratinocyte hyperproliferation and accelerated epidermal turnover (3-5 days instead of normal 28 days).
- Hallmark Lesion: Sharply demarcated, erythematous plaques covered with thick, cohesive, micaceous or silvery-white scales.
- Classic Predilection Sites: Extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp, lumbosacral region, umbilicus, and nails (pitting, oil-drop discoloration, subungual hyperkeratosis).
- Pathognomonic Signs:
  * Auspitz Sign: Pinpoint bleeding upon gentle scrape/removal of silvery scales.
  * Koebner Phenomenon: Development of psoriatic plaques at sites of physical cutaneous trauma (scratches, burns).

2. CLINICAL VARIANTS
- Plaque Psoriasis (Psoriasis Vulgaris): 80%-90% of cases.
- Guttate Psoriasis: Sudden eruption of small raindrop-like papules on trunk, frequently triggered by preceding Group A Streptococcal pharyngitis in youth.
- Inverse / Flexural Psoriasis: Occurs in intertriginous skin folds (axillae, groin, inframammary). Smooth, glistening, non-scaly erythema.
- Pustular Psoriasis: Sterile pustules on erythematous base (generalized or palmoplantar). Medical urgency if generalized (von Zumbusch type).
- Erythrodermic Psoriasis: >90% body surface erythema, life-threatening thermoregulatory failure.

3. MANAGEMENT STRATEGY
- Mild Plaque (<5% Body Surface Area): Potent topical corticosteroids (clobetasol, betamethasone) rotated or combined with topical vitamin D analogs (calcipotriol/calcipotriene) and keratolytics (salicylic acid 3%-5%).
- Moderate-to-Severe (>10% BSA) or Psoriatic Arthritis: Narrowband UVB phototherapy (311 nm), oral systemic agents (methotrexate, apremilast, cyclosporine), or targeted biologic therapies (anti-TNF, anti-IL-17, anti-IL-23).
